extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, psychology, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and organizes the standards and criteria the author gives for (1) when a subject counts as a science and (2) how the phenomena of mind should be studied and explained. Focuses on laws of mind, methods (association, method of agreement/difference), relationship to physiology, and related normative claims about character and freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject suitability for science
rubrics_metrics.description: Any facts are fitted, in themselves, to be a subject of science which follow one another according to constant laws, although those laws may not have been discovered, nor even be discoverable by our existing resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subject need only exhibit lawful regularities to be scientific even if the science is imperfect; examples include meteorology (laws exist but are hard to observe) and tidology (largely lawful and practically useful). The presence of constant laws, not current exactness, is the essential mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of exactness / completeness of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A science is exact when its laws comprehensively account for all causes (major and minor) influencing the phenomena; lacking that it may be an inexact or approximate science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Astronomy became exact when perturbations were accounted for; tidology is less exact because many minor/local causes are not fully ascertained. Exactness depends on the ascertainment and inclusion of subsidiary causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observability and measurability of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical predictive power of a science depends on whether the antecedent circumstances (causes) are observable, measurable, and knowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meteorology is a science though observations are incomplete; inability to obtain requisite data limits prediction even where lawful relations exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of approximate generalizations for practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate generalizations, true in the main, are often sufficient for practical and social purposes even when precise individual predictions are impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For political and social science, propositions true for the great majority are equivalent to universal ones; empirical, approximate laws combined with allowances for inaccuracy can ground expectations and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive connection to universal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To give a genuinely scientific character to approximate generalizations, they should be exhibited as corollaries from the universal laws of nature on which they rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connection shows the proper limits of approximate truths and enables derivation of propositions for new circumstances rather than mere empirical listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the laws of mind (psychology’s subject-matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of mind are the laws according to which mental phenomena (thoughts, emotions, volitions, sensations) generate one another — the uniformities of succession among states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychology studies the sequences and causal relations among mental states, whether ultimate or derivative, by observation and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between laws of mind and laws of body
rubrics_metrics.description: All states of mind are immediately caused either by other states of mind (laws of Mind) or by states of body (laws of Body/physiology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensations have bodily antecedents and belong to physiology in that proximate sense, but the successions of non-sensational mental states must be studied as mental laws; one should not infer mental laws solely from physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of direct psychological observation and experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if mental phenomena have physiological antecedents, knowledge of their succession must be sought by observing the mental phenomena themselves because we lack means to observe/characterize the relevant nervous states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject reliance solely on current physiological data; psychology must employ the ordinary methods of experimental inquiry to ascertain laws of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of association — similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar ideas tend to excite one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the fundamental associative laws that explain how ideas and memories are linked and recalled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of association — contiguity/frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: When two impressions have been frequently experienced either simultaneously or in immediate succession, then whenever one recurs it tends to excite the idea of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent conjunction (contiguity in time or space) creates associative links; examples include memory of events and habit formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of association — intensity-frequency equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater intensity in either or both impressions is equivalent, in rendering them excitable by one another, to a greater frequency of conjunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very intense single impression can create associative strength similar to many weaker conjunctions; intensity and frequency trade off in producing associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental chemistry (generation of complex ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple ideas may combine in ways analogous to chemical combination to generate complex ideas which can appear as a single, new mental state rather than a mere sum of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When component elements become inseparable in consciousness, the complex should be said to result from, or be generated by, the simple ideas. But even where generation from simples is hypothesized, the complex phenomena still require independent experimental study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of Method of Difference for causal proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere Method of Agreement (noting recurring association) is insufficient to prove causation; the method of difference (experimental variation) is required to establish that an associated element is a generating cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show that an association produces a given mental phenomenon (e.g., moral reprobation), one must test whether introducing the putative cause where it was absent produces the effect (Method of Difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent experimental study of generated phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if higher mental phenomena can be generated from simpler ones, this does not remove the need to study the higher phenomena directly by observation and experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing the simpler constituents (analogy to oxygen + sulphur) does not allow deduction of properties of the complex (sulphuric acid) without specific study; psychologists must therefore examine beliefs, desires, volitions, etc., in their own right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of bodily influences and individual susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The production of one state of mind by another is often influenced by assignable bodily states; differences between minds may be original, due to past mental history, or due to bodily (organic) constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish cases where organic differences directly change mental responses from those where they operate indirectly by altering sensations which then, via mental laws, alter higher states. Empirical analysis is required rather than crude empirical generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive limits for individuals vs aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a theoretically perfect science of human nature could not make universally precise predictions about individuals because individual antecedent data are never fully given; but aggregate/general predictions about classes or masses can be reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of social and political science rests on propositions true of large groups; where collective regularities predominate over idiosyncratic causes, predictive and explanatory power is attainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of moral freedom / character-formation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral freedom is the feeling that one can modify one's character if one wishes; a confirmed character (habit of willing) indicates practical freedom when the agent's desire would be strong enough to overcome contrary habits in particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The depressing effect of fatalism only matters where a desire exists to alter character; one must distinguish 'no desire to alter' from 'belief in inability'. Confirmed virtue (having formed and exercised the will successfully) is associated with a fuller consciousness of freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits and purposes as independent causes of volition
rubrics_metrics.description: As habits form, the action itself can become an object of desire (a purpose) and continue to be willed without reference to immediate pleasure or pain; purposes count among the causes of volitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A habit of willing (purpose) may persist even when the action ceases to be pleasurable; this explains continued practice of both hurtful excesses and resolute moral perseverance despite diminished immediate pleasure.
